As AI rapidly alters software engineering, too many leaders are treating autonomous agents as a risk to be managed, viewing the "human-in-the-loop" requirement merely as a compliance failsafe.  As we outline in our new Deloitte perspective on Agentic AI, this is a fundamental misread of the inflection point we are at.  "Human-in-the-loop" isn't a safety feature it is the defining engineering skill of the next decade.
We are moving away from the traditional Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC).  When AI agents can autonomously reason, execute, and test code, the role of the human engineer completely transforms, which means we must rebuild our engineering organizations around two new realities:
1. Engineering as Governance (The New Skill)
Our developers must evolve from "syntax typists" into "system orchestrators." The value of a senior engineer is no longer in how fast they can write a script, but in how effectively they can govern the intent, quality, and architectural trust of a multi-agent system.  Guiding and correcting autonomous agents is a completely new craft.
2. Value Velocity (The New Metric)
For decades, we measured engineering by cost, effort (story points), and volume (lines of code).  When agents handle the execution, measuring volume is meaningless.  The metric that matters now is Value Velocity - how fast can your hybrid human-agent pipeline translate a strategic business objective into a secure, deployed capability.
As tech leaders, we need to elevate our human talent to govern autonomous systems, relentlessly focusing on delivering business value.

Graduation Project Update — Final Version 
We completed our graduation project:
Learning-Based Mobile Robot Navigation in Complex Environments Using Human Demonstrations
This project focuses on teaching a mobile robot to navigate by learning from human driving demonstrations.
For the final version, we built a custom simulation environment for better data collection and testing. The floor was designed in Inkscape, while the walls and obstacles were modeled in Shapr3D and exported to Gazebo.
Using ROS2, Gazebo, RViz, TurtleBot3, Python, and PyTorch, we collected joystick demonstrations, trained the model, and tested autonomous navigation in simulation.
I mainly focused on the technical implementation, including environment design, Gazebo/RViz setup, data collection, model training/testing, and final demo preparation.
Project completed at the American University of the Middle East (AUM).
Special thanks to our supervisor Dr. Karim Youssef for his guidance and feedback, and to my team members Ali Taleb, Salman Albedaiwi, Abdullah Bourkhan, and Essa Alsalman for their work and support.
